rv.q: His Johnny Byron is truly a performance for the ages.
And since Johnny Byron is portrayed by Mark Rylance, in a seismic performance that threatens to level the old Theater, this registers as utterly natural cause and effect.
Jerusalem is theatre at its visceral, thrilling best.
The play takes wing ever more fleetly on Rylance’s astonishing exertions.
Rylance’s extraordinary performance turns Jerusalem into a must-see experience for any serious theatergoer.
Jez Butterworth's script is far too long, repetitive, and it doesn't need to be to make the point he wants it to make.
Jez Butterworth's fascinating 'Jerusalem,' imported from London to showcase the uncontainable and strenuous life-force named Mark Rylance.
Mark Rylance gives a towering performance as Johnny 'Rooster' Byron, a dissolute charmer who lives in a trailer in the woods and holds court over a ragtag collection of social misfits.
Connoisseurs of great acting won't want to miss him—but those with normal attention spans will be hard pressed to make it to the finish line.
It’s to Butterworth’s credit that we are left so conflicted by this meeting with a force of nature, in the best play of the season.

Gusts of national (or is it existential?) pride, fury, despair, and compassion blow through Jez Butterworth's galvanizing drama Jerusalem, imported to Broadway from London's Theatre with star Mark Rylance in brilliant blaze.
Rylance gives a mesmerizing, thoroughly transformative performance that will leave theatergoers in awe of his spectacular physical and vocal abilities.
The production at the Music Box is bold and high-spirited and boasts terrific acting.
Any serious theatergoer who misses an event like this should be bulldozed in favor of condos.
A child of English parents, I often cross the pond to visit relatives, so I don't think my problem with 'Jerusalem' is that I don't get it. I just don't buy it.
Rylance's titanic presence galvanizes the evening with a landmark performance.

cn.t: Critics hail Rylance's seismic, Tony-worthy performance in Butterworth's sprawling drama, though some find the three-hour play pretentious or impenetrable. Most praise its mesmerizing power and mythic exploration of vanishing rural England.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
